content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper considers the problem of finding a low-rank approximation to a kernel matrix. In the low-rank approximation problem, one would want to find a low-rank matrix such that the Frobenius distance between the low-rank matrix and the original matrix is minimized. The paper shows that this optimization problem can be upper bounded by the cost function of a Hebbian neural network with a recurrent layer. Using some experiments the paper shows that this neural network can produce accurate low-rank approximations to some synthetic datasets as well as the MNIST dataset for the Gaussian and Arc-cosine kernels.
content.main_review:
The paper sells the result as an online algorithm for finding a low-rank approximation to a kernel matrix which is not quite the right term for their algorithm. In online algorithms, one typically can only have a single pass over the input dataset while the presented algorithm needs many passes over the input until the neural network converges. 
Moreover, even though the expression of the low-rank approximation problem in terms of a neural network is novel and interesting, it would be much more compelling if the paper presented some convergence analysis for the training of the neural net. In particular, it is not clear if SGD on this network would find the optimal solution or how many epochs are needed for training the model. Basically, the paper presents an algorithm but it does not analyze the algorithm in terms of convergence, generalization, or runtime.


Minor issue:
It seems to me that you need a factor T in the term -1/2 q_i^2 f(w_i,w_i) in Eq(5).


---------------------- Score after revision -----------------------

The revised version of the paper looks better than the initial submission and it has addressed my concerns. Therefore, I raise my score to 6.

content.title: Respone to reviewer mZaz
content.comment:
Dear reviewer,

Thank you for your review!

*The paper sells the result as an online algorithm for finding a low-rank approximation to a kernel matrix which is not quite the right term for their algorithm. In online algorithms, one typically can only have a single pass over the input dataset while the presented algorithm needs many passes over the input until the neural network converges.* We are revising to clarify our use of the term “online.” We just mean that the algorithm sees only one input pattern at a time. Sometimes this term additionally includes the setting in which performance is evaluated, for example cumulative loss in a single pass through the input patterns. Our algorithm is expected to converge in a single pass through an infinite stream of input patterns. If applied to a finite batch of examples, it is true that multiple passes would be necessary for convergence. We will state this clearly in our revision.

*Moreover, even though the expression of the low-rank approximation problem in terms of a neural network is novel and interesting, it would be much more compelling if the paper presented some convergence analysis for the training of the neural net. In particular, it is not clear if SGD on this network would find the optimal solution or how many epochs are needed for training the model. Basically, the paper presents an algorithm but it does not analyze the algorithm in terms of convergence, generalization, or runtime.*
The neural net performs stochastic gradient descent-ascent (GDA). We are revising the manuscript to cite more theoretical research regarding convergence of stochastic GDA.  

*Minor issue: It seems to me that you need a factor T in the term -1/2 q_i^2 f(w_i,w_i) in Eq(5).*
Thanks, we will correct this.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper describes an online stochastic optimization of a neural network to learn an embedding such that the inner-product between embedded points approximates a non-linear kernel based similarity. This can be a radial basis function network that approximates the embedding of a Gaussian kernel. It can also use a homogeneous kernel to approximate cosine-similarities. The network approach can be seen as a sort of Nyström approximation where each output dimension is associated with a different Nyström support point (landmark). The approximation cost is in terms of minimizing an upper bound on the squared error of the similarities. Experimental results show that the method is able to learn meaningful representations.
content.main_review:
Strengths: 

The problem is interesting and follows a long line of kernel methods and scalable approximations. 

The paper's approach is well motivated. 

The paper is mostly clear and well-written. 

The results are illustrative and capture some of the nature of approximating non-linear similarities in low-dimensional space.

Weaknesses:
This approximation yields something like the Nyström method. Yet no comparisons are made to baseline the approach in terms of Nyström landmark selection algorithms such as Musco and Musco's approach "Recursive Sampling for the Nyström Method" NIPS 2017. 

The experimental results are limited but clear. Nonetheless, I'd like to see results of the performance metrics (similarity and downstream tasks) across different choices of neurons.

While the method concentrated on proper kernel methods (yielding positive semidefinite kernel matrices), it is not clear if the the PSD assumption is necessary. For example stochastic neighbor embedding (SNE) can use different kernel sizes for different input points, which doesn't maintain PSD nature.  The restriction of $f$ and their implications could be elaborated on. 

In the conclusion the wording about the discussion of the relationship to Nyström is somewhat confusing. In particular, the statement "we start with a different objective" doesn't make it clear that this paper uses the same cost as the Nyström approach, but that Fu (2014) used a different objective, which is functional approximation in the RKHS. 

Minor points: 

page 2, " OUr work" 
page 3, Aspects of the proof of Lemma 1 could be incorporated into the text.
 What is meant precisely by "nearly" convex-concave, and is it due to the nature of the Legendre transform?
page 3, comma after 2 will help the reader parse the double verbs in "is derived as an upper bound to Eq. 2 is thus" 
Figure 2 could have the variables from the paper $M,N, T$. Their choice makes them a bit hard to remember.
page 4, "gaurantee"
page 5, "Hebbian rules are been defined" 
page 5, the number of training iterations could be converted to epochs? (how many times the training data set has been seen)
content.summary_of_the_review: The paper is a solid approach to show feasible online update rules for learning representations that capture non-linear similarity.  Not all aspects of the theory or results are explored.  Key comparisons versus other scalable techniques Nyström are not made, perhaps to focus on the online nature. Nonetheless, some more comparisons and elaborations on the nature of similarities could make this approach more useful in practice.

**Weakness 1:** *This approximation yields something like the Nyström method. Yet no comparisons are made to baseline the approach in terms of Nyström landmark selection algorithms such as Musco and Musco's approach "Recursive Sampling for the Nyström Method" NIPS 2017.*
This is a great suggestion, and we are adding comparisons with several Nyström methods, including randomly sampled landmarks and k-means landmarks. Both of these methods can be implemented as online algorithms, and the latter in particular is very close to exact for Half Moons and MNIST. While the Musco and Musco algorithm has runtime linear in the number of points, their recursive sampling does not appear to qualify as an online algorithm (process a single pattern at a time)

For example stochastic neighbor embedding (SNE) can use different kernel sizes for different input points, which doesn't maintain PSD nature. We can add text to the discussion. Essentially there is no guaranteed that our method is optimizing a lower bound if you do not use a kernel. Although it is possible this method could still generate useful representations if f is not a proper kernel.

In particular, the statement "we start with a different objective" doesn't make it clear that this paper uses the same cost as the Nyström approach, but that Fu (2014) used a different objective, which is functional approximation in the RKHS.*

The reviewer is right that there is potential for confusion. We are making revisions to clarify how our bound is different from Nyström.

**Minor points:** we are working on revising these. For "nearly convex-concanve", it means the function is not necessarily convex concave everywhere, but is locally convex concave around the saddle point.

content.title: Response to reviewer yzmP
content.comment:
Dear reviewer,

Thank you for your review!

**Response to concern 1:** Chklovskii, Pehlevan, and coworkers have written numerous papers on online neural net algorithms for linear similarity matching. These are important papers, but linear similarity matching is computationally limited. Therefore it is important to extend to the nonlinear case. Sengupta et al. (2018) have introduced a similarity threshold, a constant offset into the similarity matching objective function.

Yanis Bahroun introduced an online neural algorithm for kernel similarity matching. (He informed us on OpenReview; we were not previously aware of his work.) This uses random Fourier features (RFF) to approximate a shift-invariant kernel, and then applies linear similarity matching. The RFF algorithm has the theoretical advantage of becoming exact in the limit of infinite dimension, whereas our algorithm does not. The RFF algorithm is limited to kernels that are shift-invariant, while our algorithm is more general. 

We are carrying out empirical comparisons of our algorithm versus the RFF algorithm, and will add them soon to the manuscript. So far, we are seeing that our algorithm empirically outperforms RFF for finite dimensions that are fairly large. 

**Response to concern 2:**
Compared to linear similarity matching, our algorithm is shown to be better for downstream classification. Our algorithm is not meant to outperform kernel PCA, but deliver similar performance with an online neural implementation. However, we are working on experiments to compare with other non-neural methods just to better place this method in the context of previous works.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper studies the problem of feature mapping for reproducing kernels. The focus is when the data size is too large, the SVD for the kernel Gram matrix would be prohibitively difficult. This paper proposes to use the least-squares loss to achieve a low-rank approximation to the Gram matrix, to use Legendre transformation to disentangle quadratic terms in the least-squares loss, and to use a two-phase Hebbian parameter update rule to achieve the approximating feature map.
content.main_review:
strength: the idea is nice. After training, the obtained function maps data points directly to their images in the feature space with low computational complexity.

My concerns:
1. The one-dimension approximation (4) may lose precision. The introduced error could be significant. Users of the algorithm may not be able to estimate the introduced error. Users may end up having a totally different reproducing kernel if they shift to using the feature images.
2. The feature map is obviously not unique. For example, for any such map x--> y=F(x), and any orthogonal matrix Q, QF(x) is exactly another feature map as good as F(x). Consequently, you can not expect that W, q, or L in (8) would converge in the first phase of training.
3. Some minor mistakes in using the Legendre transformation: the sum in t on the right-hand side of (4) does not cover (1/2)q^2f(w,w). However, we see that the author(s) made it cover this term in (5) and (6). We see that it is easy to fix this problem by scaling the term (1/2)q^2f(w,w) by 1/T.
4. The optimization problem (8) is far from convex (especially in terms of W). Compared with matured randomized matrix decomposition techniques many with convergence guarantee and designed for reducing space and time complexity (e.g. Halko, N.; Martinsson, P. G.; Tropp, J. A. Finding structure with randomness: probabilistic algorithms for constructing approximate matrix decompositions. SIAM Rev. 53 (2011), no. 2, 217--288.) (these algorithms could be plugged into kernel-based empirical feature maps to achieve the same purpose as claimed in this paper), the convergence and precision of the proposed algorithm are both difficult to verify.

========================== after reading the authors feedback
Most of my points are well addressed. I am happy to raise the score to 8. I believe that combined with some regularity assumption on kernels, good theoretical results can be derived for the proposed algorithm as future work.

content.title: Response to reviewer qZPh
content.comment:
Dear reviewer, 

Thank you for your review!

**Response to point 1:** It is true that our algorithm depends on an approximation. To evaluate the precision of the approximation, we provide some empirical comparisons. Figures 4 and 6 show that the kernel similarities f(x_s, x_t) closely match the feature similarities y_s dot y_t for the Half Moons problem and for MNIST. Also, for linear kernels at least, this rank 1 approximation is sufficient (the optimal bound yields an inequality for the linear kernel).

**Response to point 2:** For the objective in Eq. 1, any orthogonal transform of the learned $y$ will yield the same energy. We are optimizing not Eq. 1, however, but the lower bound of Eq. 5. This lower bound in general breaks the continuous degeneracy when the kernel is nonlinear. 
If there is concern about convergence, it should be for a different reason. Our neural algorithm uses gradient descent-ascent (GDA), for which the convergence guarantees are not as strong as pure gradient descent or pure gradient ascent. We will expand our discussion of convergence, and citations of the relevant theoretical works on convergence.

**Response to point 3:** Thanks for pointing this out. We are revising and will fix this.

**Response to point 4:** We are revising the manuscript to be more explicit about our desiderata for algorithms. Our most basic requirement is that

(A) We want an algorithm that doesn’t have to explicitly compute every element of the similarity matrix. 

The reason for requirement A is that the NxN similarity matrix is huge when the number of input patterns N is large. The dimension reduction algorithms of Halko et al. (2011) require at least one pass through every element of the similarity matrix, violating requirement A. In Section 2.1, Halko et al. (2011) mention in passing the alternative sparsification and column selection approaches. These randomly sample elements or columns to yield a surrogate matrix that can be factorized. Superficially, these alternative approaches might seem to obviate the one pass through the similarity matrix. It turns out, however, that one pass is still required to compute the sampling distribution. Therefore, as far as we can tell, all of the randomized matrix decomposition techniques of Halko et al. (2011) violate requirement A.
Our algorithm satisfies requirement A, and in addition satisfies two other requirements:

(B) We want an online algorithm, meaning that a single input pattern suffices for each learning update.

(C) We want an algorithm that is implemented as a biologically plausible neural network. 

We were willing to sacrifice some precision for the sake of these requirements, and the empirical results show that the sacrifice is not so large in two example cases.

Kernel Similarity Matching was introduced in these exact terms in [1] and [2] for clustering and nonlinear dimensionality reduction. None of these two works were cited here. content.title: Response to Authors
content.comment:
Hi,

First of all, I would like to reiterate that in my opinion this work is novel and complements a variety of existing work. I personally really enjoyed reading it. I think that this work also has a lot of potential in connection with Neuroscience. The SM framework has proved useful for modeling a variety of neural structures [1-2] and for unsupervised and supervised learning tasks [3-4] and this work certainly proposes a way forward. 

Question 1: 
In that work, I used kernel nonnegative similarity matching for a clustering task. How it was shown in the original work of Pehlevan et al. [5] the output is sparse but not exactly winner-take-all, thus when comparing to other methods, it is important to acknowledge that and when measuring the performance, I used the maximal response neuron as an assignment. 
It is in my thesis that I provided some quarantine and proof of concept for Kernel Unconstraint Similarity Matching, which is the offline objective that you also proposed. Your work is more exhaustive and the experiments you present very compeling. 

Question 2:
Yes, indeed it amounts to that. The doctoral thesis of [6] provides a great description of a variety of competing models that can be efficiently be trained online. The respective papers forming the thesis were cited in my work. 


[1] Lipshutz, David, et al. "A Biologically Plausible Neural Network for Multichannel Canonical Correlation Analysis." Neural Computation 33.9 (2021): 2309-2352.

[2] Bahroun, Yanis, Dmitri Chklovskii, and Anirvan Sengupta. "A similarity-preserving network trained on transformed images recapitulates salient features of the fly motion detection circuit." Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 32 (2019): 14201-14212.

[3] Obeid, Dina, Hugo Ramambason, and Cengiz Pehlevan. "Structured and Deep Similarity Matching via Structured and Deep Hebbian Networks." Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 32 (2019): 15403-15412.

[4] Qin, Shanshan, Nayantara Mudur, and Cengiz Pehlevan. "Contrastive Similarity Matching for Supervised Learning." Neural Computation 33.5 (2021): 1300-1328.

[5] Pehlevan, Cengiz, and Dmitri B. Chklovskii. "A Hebbian/anti-Hebbian network derived from online non-negative matrix factorization can cluster and discover sparse features." 2014 48th Asilomar Conference on Signals, Systems and Computers. IEEE, 2014.

[6] Chitta, Radha. Kernel-based clustering of big data. Michigan State University, 2015.

content.title: Paper Decision
content.comment:
This paper studies the problem of kernel similarity matching using Hebbian neural networks. Specifically, the authors propose to compute the approximate feature map for the kernel using the least square loss function, Legendre transformation, and Hebbian parameter update rules.

Reviewers generally agree that the proposed method is interesting. However, there are major issues with the current manuscript, both theoretically and empirically. Theoretically, there is no guarantee for the convergence of the method. In fact, the non-convergence of the approximation error, when the dimensionality (number of features) increases, indicates that the proposed method is not consistent, in contrast with other methods such as Kernel PCA or Nystrom approximation-based methods. As observed by the authors, this may be related to the unstable convergence of the stochastic gradient descent ascent optimization procedure. For consistency,
the approximation error needs to approach zero as the number of features becomes large. 
Overall, empirical results compared with existing methods are not  satisfactory. As the authors themselves point out in their discussion, "this method does not provide the same sorts of theoretically guarantees or empirically observed robustness of sampling based methods".

The authors are encouraged to take  reviewers' comments and suggestions into account to improve their current work.
